title: Viral Robot Malfunctions at Beijing Conference Undercut China's Push to Prove Humanoids Are Ready for Work
excerpt: Robots glitching at the World Robot Conference come at an awkward moment for an industry trying to move past crowd-pleasing demos to commercial deployment.
body:
• Viral video from the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing showed humanoid robots malfunctioning during demonstrations, with operators struggling to regain control.
  • The incidents come at a critical moment for China's humanoid industry: Unitree's IPO soared 460% on debut, 300+ companies are exhibiting, and investor enthusiasm is at an all-time high.
  • Industry leaders acknowledge that robots remain less efficient than human workers, with 50-70% of humanoids produced this year likely ending up in data-collection facilities rather than productive commercial roles.
  • The U.S. has added foreign-made humanoid robots to an FCC import restriction list, adding geopolitical pressure to China's push for rapid commercialization.

The timing could hardly have been worse. As China's World Robot Conference opened in Beijing this week — the country's premier showcase for an industry that has captured billions in investor capital — viral video of humanoid robots malfunctioning on the conference floor spread rapidly across social media.

Footage showed robots experiencing erratic, seizure-like movements during demonstrations, with operators scrambling to intervene and restore control. The incidents added an uncomfortable counterpoint to the polished presentations happening elsewhere at the five-day event, which runs through Sunday.

A $50 Billion IPO Meets Reality

The malfunctions came on the same day that Unitree, one of China's best-known humanoid robot makers, made a spectacular stock market debut. Shares of the company surged 460% on the Shanghai STAR Market, closing at 845 yuan after an IPO that was more than 8,000 times oversubscribed by retail investors. The listing valued Unitree at approximately $50 billion.

https://x.com/nexta_tv/status/2090470413327532291

More than 300 mostly domestic companies are attending the conference, displaying over 2,000 exhibits and launching more than 150 products, according to Beijing authorities. The event is meant to signal that Chinese robotics has matured beyond viral demonstrations — breakdancing robots, marathon-running machines, flying-kick performances — toward commercial viability.

"The onus is on the humanoid players to show we have a solution. The robots need to be affordable, safe, and ready to use."

— Jeff Burnstein, president of the Association for Advancing Automation

The Gap Between Demo and Deployment

Unitree founder Wang Xingxing, addressing the conference the day after his company's blockbuster debut, acknowledged the fundamental challenge: robots are not yet as efficient as humans and take time to learn new skills, creating a bottleneck for the industry. Unitree shares fell 18.7% the following day.

Georg Stieler, a Berlin-based robotics analyst who advises industrial companies in China, estimates that 50% to 70% of humanoid robots produced this year will end up in "data factories" — facilities where machines collect training data rather than perform productive work for paying customers.

The economics remain unfavorable. A Chinese brokerage, Guotai Securities, estimates an industrial humanoid would need to cost about 160,000 yuan, including maintenance, to pay for itself within two years compared with a worker earning 80,000 yuan annually. Most such robots currently cost 300,000 to 500,000 yuan, according to Berlin-based think tank MERICS.

A Pattern of Public Failures

Robot malfunctions at public events have become a recurring theme in China's robotics push. Earlier this year, a Qualcomm-powered humanoid collapsed face-first during a live demonstration at Computex 2026 in Taipei. At CES 2026 in Las Vegas, multiple Chinese-made robots malfunctioned during demonstrations. In previous years, incidents at Chinese festivals and campus events have involved robots lurching toward crowds or grabbing bystanders, prompting calls for stricter safety protocols.

Safety experts say the more important question is not why robots malfunction — software glitches, signal interference, and sensor failures are expected at this stage of development — but why malfunctioning machines are still able to operate in proximity to people without adequate failsafe mechanisms.

Geopolitical Headwinds

The industry's growing pains are colliding with geopolitical pressure. Last month, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission added foreign-made advanced robotic devices, including humanoids, to a list restricting imports to the United States. While previously authorized models can still be sold, the move affects companies including Unitree.

Technology research firm IDC estimates China accounts for 82% of global humanoid shipments. Under its worst-case scenario for the U.S. restrictions, American humanoid sales would be 58% below IDC's prior baseline forecast by 2030.

China delivered over 40,000 humanoids in the first half of this year alone, according to a Chinese humanoid industry body. Beijing is betting that robots can eventually replace human labor as the country faces a shrinking workforce due to demographic decline. But this week's conference has made one thing clear: between investor hype and factory-floor reality, the gap remains wide.
